::: {.lede}
My work follows one chain of cause and effect: how the food we eat is recorded
in the epigenome and physiology of fat tissue, how that record sets the tissue's
capacity to store and mobilize energy, and how that capacity shapes long-term
metabolic health.
:::

::: {.stage-section}
[Nutrition]{.stage-label}
## Diet as a signal {.stage-heading}

Diet is more than fuel — specific nutritional states act as signals. Across my
work, cues such as fasting, ketogenesis, and the availability of sulfur amino
acids like methionine reprogram metabolic tissues. As an EMBO postdoctoral
fellow I focused on dietary methionine as a signal to thermogenic fat (the
*ChromaBAT* project), asking how a nutrient becomes an instruction.
:::

::: {.stage-section}
[Adipose epigenome]{.stage-label}
## Writing the chromatin record {.stage-heading}

These dietary signals converge on chromatin. I study how nutritional state is
written into the gene-regulatory landscape of fat cells — for example, how
restricting dietary sulfur amino acids elicits a cold-like transcriptional
program in white adipose tissue. The recurring question is how a transient
dietary input leaves a durable regulatory mark.
:::

::: {.stage-section}
[Storage capacity]{.stage-label}
## Setting the limits of energy storage {.stage-heading}

That regulatory state determines what fat tissue can do: how it takes up,
stores, and releases lipid. My earlier work dissected the machinery controlling
lipoprotein lipase — how ANGPTL4 drives its intracellular cleavage by
PCSK3/furin, and how fasting raises ANGPTL4 to lower LPL activity in human
adipose tissue — alongside how ketone bodies such as β-hydroxybutyrate signal
within muscle and fat.
:::

::: {.stage-section}
[Health & aging]{.stage-label}
## Consequences across the lifespan {.stage-heading}

Energy-storage capacity shapes metabolic health over a lifetime. I work to
connect mechanism to physiology — from hepatic fatty-acid oxidation and
ketogenesis during fasting to the metabolic regulation and safety of long-term
fasting in humans — with a growing interest in aging and metabolic resilience.
:::
